item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
1) If I were writing this today, I probably would have used the classification you mention. Roughly, the doll, as the actual object in question, would be the primary designation, while the apparition is something SCP-136 produces.

2) Yep, that's too big. 10 x 10 x 10m rooms were kind of a thing, back then. Probably should have just been a "standard [make up some designation] containment cell," as the exact dimensions aren't relevant for containment. Ideally, containment procedures should be the vital information you need while leaping out of a helicopter to deal with a breach, and "exact size of the room" doesn't really qualify.

3) Should have been Safe, because "lock it in a box" was good enough to contain it. The incident reports are supposed to show that it's more unpredictable than originally assumed, and that it does occasionally manifest to people without having looked at the doll. Properly speaking, it probably should have been reclassified to Euclid or Keter when that happened, because containment procedures became unreliable. The whole "but we're using it for EVIL" schtick at the end there is not really done anymore, for good reason — any cruelty on the Foundation's part should be impersonal and clinical, not "comic book villain."

Looking back… yikes. I was one hell of an edgy teenager (and not a very good writer) back when I came up with this one, wasn't I?

Bearing in mind that this article is 9 years old and probably not necessarily still in line with current SCP expectations, I have the following queries (which are for the purposes of aiding my own understanding of how SCP stuff works as much as anything):
1. Should the doll be SCP-136 and the apparition SCP-136-1? Otherwise you're just trying to contain a 'phenomenon' which seems rather nebulous
2. A 1000 cubic meter concrete containment room? Really? Seems a tad on the large side, especially when…
3. You could just lock the thing in a filing cabinet, reclassify it as Safe, and be done with it? Unless I'm missing something there's no real evidence that the doll moves around of its own volition unless it's damaged

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: the face, as described as 'a rictus of pain and arousal', is actually very hard to visualize. Given that both of those emotions are often accompanied by the baring of teeth, but SCP-136-2 is implied to keep its mouth closed the majority of the time, the closest approximation might be a malevolent smile. The most recognizable trait of an aroused expression is heavy lidded eyes, while pained expressions usually are depicted with eyes closed. The juxtaposition of pained eyes but smiling lips is an option, as is a potential closed lipped grimace at odds with the sultry expression of the other features. Basically what I'm getting at is that significant artistic license would have to be used unless more details are provided.

item.title: Good buildup

Perhaps some specific phobia to dolls, or something similar?
